Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Architect
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Vignette:
Layla was an 18-year-old Arab American woman in the first year of architectural training, already spending long days in a studio where late hours, draft tables, and the constant rustle of movement around her were treated as normal. She came to treatment after months of feeling as though her body never stood down from alarm. She described herself as exhausted and tense at the same time, single, living at home, and increasingly unable to move through ordinary days without a sense that something terrible might happen again.

The event she returned to when asked why she no longer felt safe had happened several months earlier on an ordinary afternoon in the city. She had been leaving a building after class, still carrying sketch rolls and a laptop case, when shouting broke out on the sidewalk nearby. She looked up in time to see another person being violently attacked. What stayed with her was not only the sight of the assault itself but the suddenness of it: one moment people were walking past storefronts and traffic was moving as usual, and then there was panic, screaming, bodies backing away, and the terrible realization that she was close enough to see the victim’s fear. She remembered freezing and feeling useless, horrified that she was watching someone suffer and unable to make it stop. Even after other people intervened and emergency sirens arrived, she was left with the conviction that safety could disappear without warning in the middle of a normal day.

In the weeks afterward, Layla found that her emotional life had narrowed around intense fear, horror, anger, and guilt. She could still picture how exposed the victim had looked, and she felt ashamed that she had stood there stunned rather than doing something decisive. At other times she became angry—at the attacker, at the people who had kept moving at first, and at herself for having believed public places were basically safe. She had come to feel that her reactions were not excessive but appropriate to what she had learned: if something like that could happen in front of her in daylight, then danger had to be watched for constantly.

That sense of constant watchfulness followed her into the architecture studio. The room was busy and open, with students crossing behind one another, doors opening unexpectedly, and people drifting in late at night to finish projects. Layla no longer experienced that bustle as background. She tracked who came in, where people were standing, and whether voices in the hallway sounded agitated. If classmates laughed suddenly or raised their voices during critique, her body tensed before she could think. She often positioned herself where she could see the entrance, telling herself that it was irresponsible not to stay aware. During long studio nights, while others bent over models with headphones on, Layla kept scanning the room and the corridor beyond it. She knew this made it harder to concentrate, but being less alert felt dangerous, almost reckless.

Sleep became another battleground. At night she was tired enough to cry from it, yet she delayed going to sleep because she felt she needed to remain on guard. Lying in bed, she listened for sounds in the house, for cars outside, for footsteps, for anything out of place. If she began to drift off, she sometimes pulled herself back awake with the thought that letting go meant becoming vulnerable. She did not describe restful nights anymore; instead she described negotiations with herself—just a little longer, just until the house is completely quiet, just until I’m sure nothing is wrong. By morning she was depleted, and the exhaustion made the next day in studio feel even more strained.

Over time these patterns altered how she lived. Family members noticed that she startled at minor noises and seemed perpetually braced. In school, she remained capable and serious, but assignments took longer because so much of her attention was spent monitoring the environment rather than settling into design work. She felt embarrassed by how frightened she was and guilty that the person she had witnessed suffering was the one who had truly been harmed, yet she could not make herself stop scanning. What frightened her most was the possibility that this constant alarm meant the world really was as unsafe as it now seemed, and that if she relaxed even briefly she would again be caught in the instant when ordinary life turned violent.

She sought help after recognizing that she was no longer just remembering what happened; she was organizing her days and nights around the possibility of another threat. By the time she came in, she was worn down by sleeplessness, ashamed of how much fear and guilt she carried, and discouraged that even in a classroom devoted to creativity she could not stop watching the door. She said she wanted help because she missed feeling young and absorbed in her work, but she was also afraid that if she stopped being vigilant, something irreversible would happen and she would once again be left standing there, horrified and unable to protect anyone.
